lessons.title: Rama Natha and the Magic Potion

activities.prompt: What happens when a potion seeker follows a famous sage?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Potion Search
activities.body:
You are Rama Natha, the son of a rich landlord. When your father dies, he leaves you large areas of land. Yet you do not look after the land for even one day. Instead, you believe a magic potion can turn any object into gold. You spend all your time learning more about the potion.

Many people often cheat you by promising to tell you about the potion. You spend money on the search, hoping to learn its secret. Your wife, Madhumati, becomes tired and worried about your search. She worries about the large amount of money you spend. She thinks you will soon have no money left.

Then, a famous sage named Mahipati comes to your town. You follow the sage and ask about the potion. Even so, you do not stop trying to find the potion.

Your land remains uncared for while your thoughts stay with the potion. Madhumati keeps worrying about your search and your spending. Your determination continues, and she believes you will soon have no money left.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

lessons.title: The Sage's Instructions

activities.prompt: What would you do if a sage asked for a bottle of morning dew?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Sage's Dew Task
activities.body:
You had to plant a banana plant. You had to water the plant regularly, using your hands.

On winter mornings, dew rested on the leaves. You had to collect this dew and store it in a bottle.

Your task was to bring the sage five litres of dew. He said that he would chant magic words. The collected liquid would become a magic potion.

A drop of this potion could change any object into gold. Rama Natha thought it would take years to collect the dew. Yet winter lasted only for a few months.

You could plant as many banana plants as you wanted. You still had to look after the plants and collect the dew yourself. The plants and their dew were your responsibility.

One drop could turn any object into gold.

lessons.title: Six Years of Hard Work

activities.prompt: How can patient care turn an empty field into something amazing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Six Years of Hard Work
activities.body:
You find Rama Natha beside his fields. You watch him speak to his wife before he begins cleaning them. The fields have lain empty for many years. Yet he starts this patient work with care.

He plants rows and rows of banana plants. You see him look after every plant carefully. During winter, he collects the dew with great care. After six years, he has five litres of dew.

Madhumati also helps him. You watch her gather the banana crop and take it to the market. They receive a good price for the bananas. Each year, Rama Natha plants more banana plants.

Gradually, a huge banana plantation grows. You now see why six years of careful work matter. Rama Natha carefully takes the bottle to the sage.

You watch the sage smile and mutter something over the water.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.body: Rama Natha spoke to his wife before cleaning his empty fields. He planted banana plants and cared for them carefully. Madhumati helped gather the crop and took it to market. They got a good price. Each year, they planted more plants and grew a huge plantation. After six years, Rama Natha had five litres of dew. He took it to the sage, who smiled and muttered over the water.
keyPoints: Empty fields were planted with carefully cared-for banana plants.
Madhumati helped gather the crop, and they received a good price.
After six years, Rama Natha had five litres of dew for the sage.
activities.explanation: You can see how patient work and shared help brought a huge result.

lessons.title: The Sage Reveals the Truth

activities.prompt: What was the sage really trying to teach Rama Natha?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Truth Behind the Gold
activities.body:
You follow Rama Natha to the sage with a copper vessel. He sprinkled drops of liquid onto it and waited. He expected the vessel to turn into gold, but nothing happened. He accused the sage of cheating.

Rama Natha felt that six valuable years of his life were wasted. Madhumati opened a box, and you see stacks of gold coins inside. The golden treasure offers another clue to the sage’s lesson.

The sage explained that no potion could turn things into gold. He reminded Rama Natha of the plantation he created through hard work on his land. His wife had earned money by selling the fruits in the market. Their hard work had created their wealth, not magic.

The sage knew that Rama Natha would not listen to him. That is why he admitted playing a trick. Rama Natha understood the sage’s deep message. The trick revealed that their hard work, not magic, had made them wealthy.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

The sage admitted playing a trick, and Rama Natha understood his deep message.
keyPoints: The copper vessel did not turn into gold.

The sage admitted a trick, and Rama Natha understood the message.
activities.explanation: This story shows how hard work can create real wealth.

lessons.title: Reflecting and Learning New Words

activities.prompt: What can you discover while following a potion story?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Lesson in Words
activities.body:
You meet Rama Natha in this story. People often cheat Rama Natha. He continues trying to learn about the potion. You follow his efforts closely.

Madhumati is tired and worried about Rama Natha’s behaviour. You see her concern beside his effort to learn. The sage smiles and mutters something over the water. You watch the sage.

The sage returns the bottle and asks Rama Natha to try it. Rama Natha sprinkles drops on a copper vessel and waits. You watch the vessel carefully. The copper vessel does not turn into gold.

You turn to the example sentences. Both example sentences contain the letter ‘b’. You look for this letter in each sentence. In the active sentence, Bunty bhaiya is the buyer. In the passive sentence, the bunch of bananas is the focus.

You meet homophones. Homophones have the same sounds but different spellings and meanings. Words with the same sounds but different meanings are called homophones. You now have this new word to use. You reflect on the potion story and this word lesson.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

keyPoints: Rama Natha kept trying to learn about the potion.

Homophones have the same sounds but different meanings.
activities.explanation: These details help you reflect on the story and learn new words.

activities.prompt: Who will you meet, and what will you share?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Madhumati's Banana Journey
activities.body:
You are Madhumati, and you are happy. You have many big bags of bananas. Your day begins with a journey. You visit your mother first. After that, you go to the market. Then you return home.

Your first stop is your mother's. You give her two dozen bananas. This is the first sharing of your banana collection. You give from the many big bags you have. The visit comes before the market trip. Your journey then continues.

Next, you go to the market to sell the bananas. This trip has a clear purpose. The market also brings another person into your journey. You meet your old friend Kalawati. She is there in the market, and your meeting becomes a sharing moment.

You give Kalawati a dozen bananas. This is another gift of bananas that day. You have shared with your mother and now with your old friend. Your journey then turns towards home. On your way home, you meet a hungry little boy. The last part of this journey brings you this hungry little boy.

activities.title: Gajaraj’s New Friend
activities.body:
You live in the best booth of the royal stables, where Gajaraj is cared for. The king is fond of him and orders him to be well looked after. Gajaraj is well cared for, yet he feels lonely. He is sad because he has no friends.

The mahout is the only person who interacts with Gajaraj. He is kind and cares for him well. Still, the mahout is not his friend. Gajaraj receives excellent care, but he has no companion to share his days.

One late evening, a dog comes into the stable by mistake. It wags its tail to show Gajaraj its thanks. The mahout notices that Gajaraj likes the dog’s company. For a while, Gajaraj is not alone. Gajaraj now has the dog for company.

Now, picture joining Gajaraj for a bath. Buntee goes with the elephant, and you come along too. As you watch, Gajaraj enjoys the dog’s company. The mahout notices that Gajaraj likes having the dog nearby.

activities.title: When Friends Part
activities.body:
You see Gajaraj pick Buntee up with his trunk. He places Buntee on his back. Buntee is happy to get a ride.

You know the farmer has been looking for Buntee since he disappeared. The farmer hugs Buntee. You watch him put a rope around Buntee’s neck.

You watch Buntee realise that the farmer is taking him away from Gajaraj. Gajaraj and Buntee are both sad. You understand that they are being separated.

The farmer tells Buntee to go to Gajaraj if he misses him. You watch the farmer remove the rope that held Buntee. You know Buntee may go to Gajaraj if he misses him.

Gajaraj leaves his lunch untouched. That night, he does not eat his food. Buntee also does not eat at the farmer’s house. You remember that Gajaraj and Buntee are both sad.

activities.title: A Friend’s Prayer
activities.body:
You imagine standing beside a speaker who names what matters most. Friendship remains the most important thing in her life. You learn that she feels blessed whenever she has special friends. You see how deeply she values these friendships.

She wants to do more than share the hopes and plans of caring friends. She wants to share the hopes and plans of friends who care. You picture her trying to do everything that a good friend can do. You sense the care behind this promise.

She wants to make her friends’ wishes come true. You see that she wants to do more than share their hopes and plans. She wants to share the hopes and plans of friends who care. Together, these wishes show what friendship means to her.

She does not want to judge her friends from far away. She wants to love her friends just as they are. You are invited to use your heart to understand what friendship can be. You understand why friendship remains so important to her.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Wishes for Friendship
activities.body: The speaker asks for friendship to stay most important in her life. Blessed means feeling thankful for something good. She feels blessed with special friends. She wants to love friends as they are. She wants to share their hopes and plans. She wants to understand friendship with her heart. She will try everything a good friend can do. Her deepest wish is to help friends’ wishes come true.

activities.title: The Invisible Chair
activities.body:
You meet Mario, who loved having lots of friends. He often boasted about them. He said that he was friendly with everyone at school. You listen as his confidence fills the air.

His grandfather offered him a bet involving fruit chaat. The grandfather said that many of Mario’s schoolmates were only companions or partners. You now wonder how Mario would answer this.

The grandfather gave Mario a special chair. It was kept in the attic. The chair was invisible and difficult to sit on. You follow the strange lesson towards its surprising test.

Mario asked everyone to form a circle. On his first attempt, he missed the invisible chair and fell. You watch the attempt closely and hold your breath.

Finally, Mario tried again and did not fall. You leave the story thinking about the invisible chair, the bet, and Mario’s boastful words.

activities.title: The Chair Test
activities.body:
You join the children for a chair test. Mario finally sits on an invisible chair in mid-air. He falls.

Guneet, Asma and Deepa hold Mario up so he will not fall. But the other children laugh at Mario’s falls. True friends are people who care for us. They do not enjoy another person’s bad luck.

Anyone who passes the chair test becomes a friend for life. It is also a chance to learn words. A suffix comes after a root word. Words describing a person’s or thing’s quality are adjectives.

Later, you meet Manu and Monika. Monika is a supportive friend. She guides Manu, introduces her to others and shares her notes. She is always there for Manu. Her help and support create a good friendship. You can recognise true friendship through Monika’s actions.

lessons.title: The Names of Neem

activities.prompt: Why has the neem tree gained so many names?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Names of Neem
activities.body:
Imagine you are standing beside a neem tree, curious about its many names. People have called this useful tree in different ways. Nimba and Nimbaca were Sanskrit names, while Iranians gave the name Neem. In Hindi, neem is called Nimb.

One Sanskrit name, Arishta, means the one who cures diseases. You may also hear Leemba, Nimori, Nimbamond, Nimbe and Nimo. These are other Indian names for the same tree. Trees become well known because of what they do. Neem is well known because people find it useful.

Scientists call neem the bitter grace of God. They also call it nature’s gift to man and the cleanliness-parting tree. Some people call neem the magic tree. Neem is also called the tree of the twentieth century. People know neem because they find it useful.

As you walk away, you may look at the tree with new respect. You now know why people give neem so many names. Its usefulness helps make the tree well known. Perhaps you will remember neem and its many names.

In Hindi, neem is called Nimb. Other Indian names include Leemba, Nimori, Nimbamond, Nimbe and Nimo. Scientists call neem the bitter grace of God and nature’s gift to man.

activities.title: Neem as Medicine
activities.body:
Imagine visiting a village where neem trees grow around the homes. You see people cleaning their teeth with neem twigs. Neem leaves can also protect clothes from harmful insects.

Then you hear about a child with measles. Measles causes itching all over the body. A doctor advised putting neem leaves on the child’s bed. The leaves contain chemicals that destroy germs. They also give comfort and stop germs from breeding.

You learn that neem’s leaves, bark, flowers, fruits and roots can make medicines. You meet Amber. A medicine made from neem bark cured her. Kajal made from neem flowers cured Amber’s father.

Finally, you remember an important rule. These remedies should be used only by trained and experienced people. Neem can help, but the right care matters.

Trained people should use these remedies.

activities.title: Neem on Farms
activities.body:
You visit a farm where neem helps protect plants. Farmers can mix neem seed powder in water. Then they spray the mixture on their plants. Neem seed powder gives farmers a useful plant spray.

Locusts will not eat plants sprayed with neem seed powder. So the sprayed plants stay safe from locusts. You watch the farmer prepare the spray in water. The liquid is then used on the plants.

You move to rice fields where water remains standing. Neem can be used in these wet fields. Farmers can choose neem for their rice crops here. You see water around the plants as you tour the farm.

Termites eat the roots of crops. Neem saves crops from termites. You learn how neem can also stop other crop-eating insects from breeding.

You find stagnant water around homes. Neem seed powder can be put into this water. It stops mosquitoes from breeding. This is also a cost-effective way to stop mosquitoes from breeding. Neem can also help increase the crop yield.

It saves crop roots from termites. It is a cost-effective way to stop mosquito breeding.

activities.title: Neem Around You
activities.body:
Imagine that you are visiting a grain store. You watch neem seed powder being mixed with the stored grains. This helps protect them from insects.

You then visit a place where neem oil is used to make soap. Next, you see neem oil being used to make toothpaste. Both are products made with neem oil.

After that, you look at a wooden chair and a table. They can be made from neem wood. Termites do not eat neem-wood furniture. You can admire this useful wood.

Now you step into a room with neem trees nearby. You take a deep breath and think about how neem purifies the air. You notice how this tree helps the place around it.

Finally, you imagine yourself older. Many qualities of neem have yet to be discovered. Amber hoped to discover more qualities when she grew up. Perhaps you will help find them too.

activities.title: The Changed Score
activities.body:
You always wanted to win. You could not accept losing, even when playing marbles. You refused to play whenever you thought you would lose. Losing was something you found very hard to accept.

You were especially good at badminton. Surya was an excellent badminton player too. Your coach organised friendly matches on the last Friday of every month. Then, you and Surya were chosen to play against each other.

You were told to keep the score. Surya seemed relaxed during the match. You saw him win points and keep joking. You still wanted to win. Your wish to win stayed strong throughout the game.

You secretly changed the scoreboard. This act of cheating gave you the victory you wanted. You won the match, but not through honest play. Your earlier wish to win had guided your choice.

Look again at what happened. You were especially good at badminton, yet you still cheated. You always wanted to win, and that wish remained strong. The scoreboard recorded your victory, but the victory came through cheating.

activities.body:
You noticed that Surya was good at some things but poor at others.

The next day, you watched him play again.
For ten minutes, he could not score a basket.
He kept smiling while the basketball game continued.

You realised that a game did not need a scoreboard.
It did not need a tally of scores either.
Enjoying the game was the important thing.
Trying to do well mattered just as much.
Together, these thoughts changed how you saw sport.

After this, you began playing hide and seek.
You felt sad whenever hide and seek was about to end.
You also began joking while playing badminton.
The other students began praising your sporting spirit.

You looked back and remembered Surya’s smile.
You had seen that poor results did not stop him enjoying basketball.
You knew that a game could be enjoyable without a scoreboard.
You knew that trying to do well also mattered.
Then you began playing, joking, and showing your sporting spirit.

activities.title: Evening Turns to Night
activities.body:
You watch the children playing ball in the evening. They play beside a creek in a neighbour’s field. The game is Kho-kho, an indigenous game. The children run very fast while they play. Soon, they cannot catch their breath.

The sky is blue at first, but it slowly changes into black. The cold grass makes their feet ache. You watch the game fade as evening turns towards night.

By then, the children are out of breath and their feet ache. Still, they run very fast beside the creek. The game ends when night begins. Night is the winner, just as the poem shows.

The poem gives human qualities to non-human things. Night acts like a champion because the game ends when night begins. You see the sky change, feel the cold underfoot, and notice their racing steps.

Evening play cannot outrun the winner, because night has already won. The story ends with the children stopping as night begins.

activities.title: A Journey Through Yoga
activities.body:
Imagine standing in ancient India. You are about to begin a journey with yoga. This physical, mental and spiritual practice unites your mind and body. It also brings your thoughts and actions together.

You learn that the Sanskrit root of Yoga is 'yuj'. Patanjali presented this tradition in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. Its purpose includes quieting your mind and removing distractions. You also explore harmony between humans and nature.

Now you move through yoga postures. They help stretch and strengthen your muscles. They also improve your flexibility, endurance and balance. This supports a complete approach to health and well-being.

Next, you focus on breathing techniques and meditation. These practices improve your sleep and concentration. Concentration is also improved through yoga. As distractions quiet, your thoughts and actions become united.

Finally, you see why yoga has become popular around the world. Its health benefits explain this popularity. You remember that yoga supports harmony between humans and nature. You leave with mind and body working together.

activities.body:
You meet a girl. Her grandfather has practised yoga since he was sixteen. Your journey begins with two useful words. “Practice” is a noun. It shows the actual exercise of a skill. “Practise” is a verb. It means doing an activity repeatedly. You can begin practising yoga whenever you choose. “Advice” is a noun, while “advise” is a verb.

Now picture yourself opening the WHO mYoga app. It was launched on 20 June 2021. The app contains videos and audio files. It is an easy-to-use and free tool for people everywhere. You can begin practising yoga at any time.

During yoga, you practise asanas. Each stretch includes breathing and awareness. Your mind must be involved when you practise yoga asanas. Your body, breathing and awareness work together.

Next, you think of the UN General Assembly. It had 193 members when it accepted the proposal. The accepted proposal named 21st June as International Yoga Day. You now see yoga’s worldwide reach. It reaches people through an app and a special day.

activities.body:
Imagine beginning a journey across Bharat, a land known worldwide for wise and heroic people. You may have seen pictures of green forests, rivers, lakes and high mountains.

Travellers have come since ancient times, attracted by Bharat's rich and diverse culture. You might hear many languages and enjoy different cuisines. Music, dance, theatre, movies and films add more variety. You find different languages, cuisines, cultures and traditions all around you.

Yet, something lovely holds this variety together. You see people living together in unity while keeping their diversity. The Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme helps you interact with people. It promotes mutual understanding between people of different states and Union Territories.

It celebrates unity in diversity and strengthens emotional bonds. You see how different cultures are connected, supporting nation-building. It also highlights connections between various cultures and traditions.

activities.title: Aipan and Dhokra
activities.body:
You meet Aakansha at a family function or festival. Aakansha draws Aipan during these gatherings. You look closely at the white rice-flour paste. It rests on brick-red walls coloured with geru. The patterns spread across floors and walls in puja rooms.

The women of the family make this folk art. You notice beautiful and mathematical designs. These designs come from cultural traditions and observations of nature.

Next, you visit Priyaranjan’s tribe. They practise Dhokra, an ancient metal craft. First, you see a figure made with clay. The clay dries before the figure is covered with wax. Fine details are carved into the wax by hand.

The wax-covered figure is then fired. Wax comes out through small openings. Melted brass scrap fills the empty space. You watch the liquid metal take the same shape as the wax model. Finally, you admire the finished Dhokra figure.

Next, you see the toys coloured with oil, water-colours, vegetable dyes and enamel paints. Their designs come from folk stories, animals, birds, bullock carts and rural life. You look closely at each chosen design.

activities.title: Up in the Air
activities.body:
Imagine a windy sky filled with flying kites. You might see them like coloured birds. The poet compares these kites to coloured birds.

In this poem, you wish to be as small and light as air. Your imagination then lifts you towards a kite. You picture climbing onto it and sailing into the air.

You drift along the kite's paper wings. You listen to the wild wind sing songs. From high above, you think it would be fun to look down. Below you, people would stand and stare.

Your view includes a park and the rooftops of a town. You seem to tour the town from the sky. Have you noticed the coloured-bird comparison? The poet uses a simile to compare the kites with coloured birds.

Think about alliteration too. Alliteration means that words begin with the same consonant sound. A kite has several main parts. These include its nose, spine, cover, line, tail and reel. A cinquain describes a person, place or thing in five lines.

activities.title: Kites Across Time
activities.body:
You arrive for a festival that people in India enjoy during Makar Sankranti. Kite flying is a tradition deeply rooted in Indian culture. This festival is called Uttarayan in Western India. Gujarat is the main centre of its celebrations.

You step onto terraces and rooftops, where people fly kites. You join kite-flying competitions with other participants. These activities show how deeply rooted the kite tradition is.

Uttarayan is also celebrated in Rajasthan and Telangana. Punjab celebrates the kite festival during Baisakhi and Basant Panchami. People also fly kites to celebrate Independence Day. Each place adds another reason for you to watch the sky.

Now you turn to ancient Indian texts and find mentions of kites. Namadeva was a thirteenth-century Marathi saint and poet. He called a kite a gudi. The word brings you back to the festival's old traditions.

In Karnataka, the Tourism Department organises the Kite Festival every year. You end your tour with a clear view of India's kite tradition.

activities.title: Art Beyond Boundaries
activities.body:
You meet Ila, an artist with colourful work. It includes cushions, bedcovers, pillows, and other lovely things.

Ila was born into a farmer's family. She could not use her hands in the usual way. Her mother and grandmother encouraged her. They taught Ila to create beautiful patterns using her feet.

Ila did not give up. She became an expert at threading a needle. She also uses a shiny needle to create beautiful designs. Kathiawar embroidery is a style that needs a great deal of skill.

You picture a state exhibition where some of her embroidery was displayed. You hear that Ila received many awards and honours for her art.

Now, you visit the National War Memorial. It was established in February 2019 as a national monument. You think about art rising above physical boundaries. Ila's embroidery shows that art can rise above physical boundaries and touch the soul.
